doc.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Legendary stride pianists who never recorded: Sam Weber, Seminole, Putney Dandridge
summary: Carter recalls obscure Harlem stride pianists and doubts that Duke Ellington took part in that circle.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: You mentioned once, and I have to admit I’m embarrassed that I’ve forgotten the gentleman’s name, but you said there was a stride pianist that used to come over from Brooklyn or from . . .

I believe it was from Brooklyn, and his name was Sam Weber [phonetic]. And, if I’m correct, he was blind or partially blind. He was quite a pianist. He used to sit in with Willy “The Lion” Smith and Fats Waller and all of those guys, and he could always hold his own, you know, with them. I believe he was Jewish, Sam Weber. I don’t know what ever happened to him. I don’t know if he ever recorded. It’s a shame if he didn’t, you know, because he was quite a player. Oh, boy, I just don’t . . . I don’t know what happened with him.
This is a name I’ve never heard anyone mention, other than you.
Really. You know, I don’t know, but I remember him quite well. Have you ever heard anybody mention the name of Seminole?
Yes, yes.
Oh, really?
Another one of these legendary pianists.
Yep, that’s right. Now, I don’t know if he ever recorded or not.
I don’t think . . . do you remember seeing him?
Oh yes, I remember seeing him, yes, and hearing him. Yeah, in Harlem, of course. He was a fine player. Do you know the name Putney Dandridge?
Yes.
Oh, you do.
The singer?
No, a piano player.
I know. Well, and he also made some vocal records.
Oh, did he make some vocal records?
Yeah, yeah, sort of like the Bob Howard style.
Oh, gee, I don’t remember. Yeah.
Was he in that stride company?
No, actually, his name came to me at the moment because I thought of him; I just don’t know quite why. But I knew him in Pittsburgh. That was about 1925.
How about the pianist Abba Labba [phonetic]?
Who?
[laughs]
Abba Labba?
Doesn’t ring a bell?
No. Where does he come in?
Another one of these . . .
Legendary characters?
. . . people that never recorded.
Abba Labba. In New York?
I believe so, yeah.
I don’t know the name, no.
Duke Ellington was very much influenced and was sort of a part of that school, you know, as a kind of a novice at the time. Do you remember him at any of these piano functions?

I don’t know. I didn’t attend many of them myself, but I would doubt if he would have been part of that, you know. He was into another thing. He was into writing, and although, you know, he could play stride piano, as we well know, but I just don’t know about his involvement with that set of people.
